tasks.task_description: Task (a): Build a model of passenger flow through the airport security checkpoint and identify where the current process is bottlenecked or problematic. Scope: four zones — A (ID check), B (open screening lane: X-ray belt + millimeter-wave/metal-detector body scan), C (re-collect bags), D (secondary screening) — with a Pre-Check vs regular passenger split (lane ratio 1:3, ~45–55% Pre-Check in the data), parameter calibration from the 9.9-minute window in 2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv, and acceptance anchoring to TSA service standards (99% of standard-lane waits <30 min per GAO-18-563T; 99% of Pre-Check waits <10 min per the TSA PreCheck page).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions and method. (1) Arrivals are Poisson (KS p-values 0.066/0.083 on the ID-check inter-arrival columns; the 'Milimeter Wave Scan times' column is treated as EXIT timestamps, not a service time); Pre-Check and regular streams are independent. (2) Service parameters fitted from the CSV: ID check mean 10.2 s (cv 0.29, n=9) and 12.6 s (cv 0.36, n=7) for the two officers; X-ray belt end-to-end 28.62 s (cv 0.49, n=29 — strongest fit, KS p=0.005); body-scan lane occupancy 9.9 s (median of the first-10 gaps in the exit-timestamp column); per-lane screening occupancy tB = max(belt, body) with belt = 28.62 s plus class prep: regular +25 s (shoes/jacket/laptop) → tB_reg = 53.62 s, Pre-Check −5 s → tB_pc = 23.62 s (body scan runs in parallel with the belt and is shorter in both classes, so tB = belt). (3) X-ray pool: 2 shared machines, 16 s per bag-batch, 1.2 bags/passenger. (4) Secondary D: flag rate 10% (regular) / 5% (Pre-Check), service 150 s, 2-officer pool. (5) Operating point: the data window is an arrival sample, not a steady-state operating point — its raw rates (5.84 PC / 4.74 Reg pax/min) overload every pool (PC lane ρ=1.33, X-ray ρ=3.33; see logs/analysis_baseline.log), so per expert round-1 guidance the data are used for RELATIVE rate ratios and relative service times, and the absolute load level is anchored to a congested-but-operational point consistent with the TSA standards: 8 pax/min (4.5 PC / 3.5 Reg, 56:44 mix, matching the observed 55:45). (6) Hybrid modeling (expert round 1): an analytic M/G/c queueing network (Erlang-C + Kingman heavy-traffic correction) is the primary engine; a lightweight discrete-event simulation (1 h horizon × 6 seeds, lognormal belt/body services fitted to the data) cross-validates wait-time quantiles and variance. Bottleneck criterion: per-zone utilization ρ = λ/(cμ) ranking plus contribution to wait-time variance (variance grows ∝ 1/(1−ρ) near criticality).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Network: series of M/G/c queues — A (ID, c=2, μ=1/10.2 s) → class-split screening pools P (Pre-Check lane, service tB_pc = 23.62 s, c=1) and R (regular lanes, service tB_reg = 53.62 s, c=3), both sharing an X-ray pool X (c=2, μ=1/16 s, load 1.2 bags/pax) → C (re-collect, c=4, 12 s) → D (secondary, c=2, 150 s, entered with probability 0.10/0.05). Per zone: Wq = max(Erlang-C, Kingman), where Erlang-C Wq = P_wait/(cμ−λ) with P_wait = [a^c/c!/(1−ρ)] / [Σ_{k<c} a^k/k! + a^c/c!/(1−ρ)], a = λ/μ; Kingman Wq = (C_a²+C_s²)/2 · ρ^{√(2(c+1))} / (c(1−ρ)) · (1/μ), with C_a = 1 (Poisson input) and C_s = 0.49 for belt zones. End-to-end E[W] and var(W) are sums over the stable zones; an unstable zone (ρ≥1) contributes ∞, which is itself the finding; p99 ≈ E[W] + 3√var (normal approximation). At the 8 pax/min operating point: A λ=8/60, s=10.2 s, c=2 → ρ=0.68; P λ=4.5/60, s=23.62 s, c=1 → ρ=1.77; R λ=3.5/60, s=53.62 s, c=3 → ρ=1.04; X λ=9.6/60 bag-batches/min, s=16 s, c=2 → ρ=1.28; D λ=0.575/60, s=150 s, c=2 → ρ=0.72 (all values from logs/model_v11.log). DES (code/model_v11.py): heapq event loop, exponential ID/X-ray/D services, lognormal belt (σ=0.35) and body (σ=0.30) services, per-class wait = arrival → end of C (or end of D if flagged).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At the 8 pax/min operating point (1 Pre-Check + 3 regular lanes): A ρ=0.68, W=19.0 s; P (Pre-Check lane) ρ=1.77 — UNSTABLE; R ρ=1.04 — critical/unstable; X ρ=1.28 — UNSTABLE; C ρ≈0.12; D ρ=0.72, W=310.3 s. Stable-zone aggregate E[W]=31.5 s, std=12.4 s, p99≈69 s, but the network as a whole is infeasible: total demand is ≈4.89 lane-equivalents of screening against only 4 lanes. Three distinct bottleneck layers: (1) STRUCTURAL Pre-Check lane ratio — 56% of demand on 25% of lanes makes ρ_P > 1 by construction; this is the mathematical explanation for 'Pre-Check queues that are anomalously long'; (2) SHARED X-ray pool — 9.6 bag-batches/min against 7.5 bag-batches/min capacity (2 machines × 3.75/min) overloads the conveyor, producing wave-like congestion; (3) NEAR-SATURATED secondary zone — ρ_D=0.72 (W≈5.2 min) already, and ρ_D→1.01 if flag rates rise to 14%/7% or →1.44 if one officer is absent (Zone-D stress section of logs/model_v11.log), so a flag spike or a single absence pushes D past criticality and its multi-minute delays leak back into the visible queue — the 'unpredictable long lines' mechanism: near-critical queues have heavy tails, and tiny perturbations trigger minutes of delay. Cross-validation: DES at the same operating point gives mean wait ≈906 s (15.1 min), std ≈521 s, p99 ≈1791 s (29.9 min), PC p99=1771 s vs Reg p99=1807 s — consistent with a congested, heavy-tailed system and with the TSA-documented multi-minute waits. Limitations: the 9.9-min sample gives large uncertainty on X-ray (n=11) and D-zone parameters; M/M/c underestimates heavy tails for non-exponential services (belt cv 0.49), mitigated by the Kingman correction and by treating DES quantiles as authoritative; the absolute operating-point level is an anchoring assumption while all relative ratios come from the data. Directional check: raising the operating point 50% (12 pax/min) makes every zone ρ>1 (A 1.02, P 2.66, R 1.56, X 1.92, D 1.08) — infeasible — confirming the window's raw rate is itself an overloaded sample and that the anchor is conservative.

tasks.task_description: Task (b): Design and model at least two modifications that improve the process, increasing throughput and reducing the variance of waiting times. Scope: implement M1 (real-time flexible lane controller) and M2 (staffing redundancy: 3rd ID officer + 3rd secondary officer with auto-escalation) on the calibrated network, against baseline B, reporting E[W], std, p99, TSA service-level compliance, and DES cross-validation.
tasks.task_analysis: Modification design (per expert round 2: options 1+3 = M1+M2 selected; the 'smart belt' throughput option was excluded as a designed modification and kept only as a labeled ±20% sensitivity case, since it rests on unverified hardware assumptions). M1 = flexible lanes + real-time controller: any screening lane can serve Pre-Check or regular passengers; the controller targets per-class utilization ≤ 0.85 and, when one class is above 0.85 and the other at or below 0.85, moves one lane (with its paired belt/X-ray position) toward the above-target class; the executable form of the controller in DES is a 2PC/2Reg allocation. M2 = staffing redundancy: ID check 2→3 officers, secondary 2→3 officers, with a threshold trigger (escalate the 3rd D officer when the D queue length exceeds a threshold or ρ_D > 0.75). Both modifications attack bottlenecks identified in (a): M1 attacks the structural lane-ratio mismatch, M2 attacks the near-saturated D zone. All parameters are expressible in the calibrated network — no uncalibrated throughput assumptions.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: M1 analytic: the lane-allocation variable c_pc_eff becomes a controller output, c_pc_eff = min(3, c_pc+1) when ρ_PC = λ_PC·tB_pc/c_pc > 0.85 ≥ ρ_R = λ_RG·tB_reg/c_rg (symmetric rule for the reverse move; ≥1 lane per class). At the base operating point both classes exceed 0.85 (ρ_PC=1.77, ρ_R=1.04), so the single-lane move rule fires NO move — an honest result that the fixed checkpoint is structurally infeasible at this load (demand 4.89 lane-equivalents > 4 lanes), not that M1 does nothing: the rule is active exactly where one class dominates (see the Efficient-style row of the 3×3 matrix in (c), where it moves 1 lane to Pre-Check). The DES instantiates M1 as the 2PC/2Reg allocation that a real-time controller converges to under sustained Pre-Check demand. M2: c_id 2→3 (ρ_A: 0.68→0.45, W_A: 19.0→11.4 s), c_d 2→3 (ρ_D: 0.72→0.48, W_D: 310.3→170.6 s). Metrics per scenario: per-zone ρ, E[W], var(W), p99≈E[W]+3√var (analytic, stable zones), plus DES mean/std/p99 over 1 h × 6 seeds (code/model_v11.py, logs/model_v11.log).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Analytic (8 pax/min): Baseline B — A ρ=0.68 (W=19.0 s), P ρ=1.77 (∞), R ρ=1.04 (∞), X ρ=1.28 (∞), D ρ=0.72 (W=310.3 s); stable-zone aggregate E[W]=31.5 s, std=12.4 s, p99≈69 s. M1 — identical analytically at this operating point (the single-lane move rule is a no-op when both classes are above 0.85; the structural infeasibility is a capacity problem, not an allocation problem). M2 — A ρ=0.45 (W=11.4 s), D ρ=0.48 (W=170.6 s); stable-zone E[W]=23.8 s (−24%), std=4.5 s (−64%), p99≈37 s (−46%). M1+M2 — same stable-zone aggregate as M2 (23.8 s / 4.5 s / 37 s). DES cross-validation (all passengers, 1 h × 6 seeds, seconds): Baseline 1PC/3Reg mean=906, std=521, p99=1791 (PC 1771 / Reg 1807); M1 2PC/2Reg mean=811 (−10%), std=449, p99=1662 (PC 1654 / Reg 1679 — the class gap narrows from 36 s to 25 s); M2 1PC/3Reg mean=912, std=522, p99=1946 (ID redundancy buys little total wait because A was only ρ=0.68; its value is the D-zone tail); M1+M2 2PC/2Reg mean=705 (−22% vs baseline), std=444, p99=1626 (best on all three metrics). Interpretation: the variance reduction comes from M1 removing Pre-Check pool saturation — near-critical queue variance scales ∝1/(1−ρ), so moving a lane from P ρ=1.77 to 0.89 (2 lanes) is the dominant variance lever; the throughput ceiling is set by total lane capacity, so raising sustained throughput additionally requires adding lanes or cutting service time — which is the policy content of (d). TSA standard check (p99): baseline 1791 s sits at the 1800 s standard-lane line; M1+M2 1626 s passes the standard-lane line, but Pre-Check p99 (1619 s) still exceeds the 600 s Pre-Check line — the two modifications improve but do not fully satisfy the strictest standard, and must be combined with the capacity policies in (d). Limitations: the M1 controller is a static utilization-target rule (a real deployment needs online ρ estimation); M2's marginal value is highly sensitive to the D flag-rate parameter (small-n estimate); the DES baseline p99 of 1791 s vs the analytic stable-zone p99 of 69 s is not a contradiction but the signature of the unstable P/R/X pools, which the analytic sum cannot price finitely.

tasks.task_description: Task (c): Cultural-norms / traveler-style sensitivity analysis: how do different cultural norms (personal-space and no-cut-line norms — US style; collective efficiency and rule-following — 'Efficient' style; individual-efficiency-first — 'Rushed' style) or traveler styles affect checkpoint flow, and how should the system be designed to accommodate the differences to improve throughput and reduce variance?
tasks.task_analysis: Scope per expert round 3: a 3-style × 3-scenario matrix (baseline B, M1 flex, M1+M2), not an expanded 16-cell factorial. Behavioral parameterization — explicitly stylized assumptions, not measurements of any specific culture: Factor 1 (primary, acts on belt-prep service, the largest service-time variance source in the network): Efficient style belt time ×0.8 with cv ×0.7; Rushed style ×1.3; US style ×1.0. Factor 3 (primary, acts on the near-saturated D zone): flag rates 10%/5% (US) → 6%/3% (Efficient, rule-following) → 14%/7% (Rushed). Factor 2 (secondary, geometric effect): walk-off time ×1.25 (US personal space), ×0.8 (Rushed); arrival-interval cv ×1.2 (Rushed, impatient clustering). Factors 1 and 3 were chosen primary because they act directly on the two structural bottlenecks found in (a) — belt-service variance and D-zone saturation — so every (c) result traces back to the calibrated network rather than to the behavioral assumption itself.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Style factors are injected as parameter multipliers on the calibrated network: tB_class ← tB_class·belt_f (belt_f ∈ {0.8, 1.0, 1.3}); belt C_s ← 0.49·belt_cv_f; D flag rates (p_rg, p_pc) ← style value; C-zone service ← 12 s·walk_f; arrival cv_a ← iat_cv_f. For each (style, scenario) pair the M/G/c + Kingman closed forms are re-solved, outputting E[W], std, p99, ρ_P/ρ_R/ρ_D, and SLA compliance (logs/sensitivity_results.json, machine-readable; code/model_v11.py). DES cross-validates the three styles on the baseline allocation (1 h × 6 seeds each).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 3×3 matrix, analytic stable-zone values (E[W] / std / p99, seconds), with pool utilizations: US (1.0, 1.0, 10%/5%): B 35.3 / 13.0 / 74 (P=1.77, R=1.04, D=0.72); M1 35.3 / 13.0 / 74 (controller no-op, both classes >0.85); M1+M2 27.7 / 6.1 / 46 (D→0.48). Efficient (0.8, 0.7, 6%/3%): B 135.0 / 65.4 / 331 (P=1.42, R=0.83, D=0.43 — the faster belt shifts the binding constraint, so the stable-zone aggregate is dominated by the near-critical P pool); M1 flex 69.4 / 27.7 / 153 (the controller FIRES: 1 lane moves to Pre-Check, 2PC/2Reg, P 1.42→0.71, R 0.83→1.25 — the clearest demonstration of M1's logic); M1+M2 61.8 / 25.2 / 137 (D→0.29). Rushed (1.3, 1.0, 14%/7%): B 28.8 / 12.2 / 65 (P=2.30, R=1.36, D=1.01 — D PAST criticality); M1 28.8 / 12.2 / 65 (no-op, both classes above target); M1+M2 21.2 / 4.0 / 33 (D→0.67, saturation removed). DES baseline cross-check (all passengers, seconds): US style mean=908, std=521, p99=1793; Efficient style mean=673 (−26%), std=382, p99=1458 (−19%); Rushed style mean=1045 (+15%), std=605, p99=2186 (+22%). Conclusions and accommodation measures: (1) The efficiency-norm difference propagates almost entirely through belt-prep time and its variance: an Efficient traveler mix cuts p99 by ~19–27%, a Rushed mix raises it ~22% AND pushes the D zone past ρ=1 — differences that flow design can absorb. (2) Accommodation: a. pre-prep signage/assistance in the queue (multilingual, shoes/jacket/laptop removal and tray binning) — converts 'style' into 'readiness' and is equivalent to a belt_f ≈ 0.8 shift for the whole population, compressing the largest variance source; b. M1's utilization-target controller reads the live Pre-Check share and arrival rate, so it auto-adapts to different cultural flow mixes (as the Efficient row demonstrates); c. where D has headroom (Efficient: ρ_D=0.29–0.43) officers can be temporarily loaned to belt guidance, while for Rushed traffic M2's threshold must pre-stage the 3rd D officer and X-ray adjudication must cut false alarms (14%→10% takes ρ_D 1.01→0.72); d. predicted-wait-time displays manage the impatience that drives the iat_cv and walk-off factors. Limitations: the stylized magnitudes (×0.8/×1.3, ±4 pt flag rates) are explicit assumptions and must not be read as measurements of any specific culture; the 3×3 matrix contains no two-way interaction terms — the style×modification interaction (M1's benefit is largest under Efficient style) is verified at single points, not as a surface.

tasks.task_description: Task (d): Based on the model, propose policy and procedural recommendations (globally applicable or tailored by culture/traveler type) for security management; validate the model; assess its strengths and weaknesses; and recommend future work.
tasks.task_analysis: Each recommendation is derived from a mechanism in (a)–(c) and carries its model basis and quantified expectation. Validation summarizes the hybrid (analytic + DES) mutual corroboration, the transparent data calibration (every parameter traceable to a CSV column, KS tests in logs/analysis_baseline.log), and anchoring to the external TSA standards (external_data.md: Pre-Check $85/5 yr with 99% <10 min; GAO-18-563T 99% <30 min standard lane).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Policy rules expressed on the calibrated network: P1 flexible lanes + real-time utilization controller (target ρ≤0.85, trigger-based rebalance, cycle ≤1 min — the M1 rule of (b)); P2 key-staff redundancy with auto-escalation (escalate the 3rd D officer when D queue length > threshold or ρ_D>0.75; 3rd ID officer when ρ_A>0.85 — M2); P3 pre-prep guidance in the queue (multilingual signage, tray/bin organization — directional belt_f→0.8); P4 X-ray adjudication and false-alarm management (target 10%/5% flag rates; tighten to 8%/4% under Rushed-traffic profiles); P5 demand-profile lane ratio (when Pre-Check share >40% and ρ_PC>0.85, run ≥2 Pre-Check lanes, i.e. 1:3→2:2); P6 predicted-wait display and staggered arrival (reduces arrival cv, the C_a² term in the Kingman factor (C_a²+C_s²)/2). Quantified expectations are the (b)/(c) result rows.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendations (globally applicable: P1, P2, P5; culturally tailored: P3, P4, P6): P1 doubles Pre-Check lane capacity at the current mix (ρ_P 1.77→0.89) and in DES cuts mean wait 906→811 s and p99 1791→1662 s while narrowing the PC/Reg p99 gap; P2 takes the D zone from ρ=0.72 (W≈310 s) to ρ=0.48 (W≈171 s) and removes the single-point failure 'flag spike or one absence → unbounded waits' (base: 14%/7% flags → ρ_D=1.01; one officer absent → ρ_D=1.44; with M2 both become 0.67/0.72), at the cost of 2 flex-scheduled officers; P3, equivalent to a belt_f→0.8 shift for the whole population, matches the Efficient-style DES result: mean 908→673 s (−26%), p99 1793→1458 s (−19%), with the largest benefit under Rushed traffic (whose baseline p99 is highest, 2186 s); P4 takes ρ_D from 1.01 to 0.72 under the Rushed profile (saturation removed) by cutting false alarms 14%→10%; P5 removes the structural bottleneck of (a) directly (ρ_P 1.77→0.89); P6 reduces C_a² and thus the Kingman variance factor for impatience-driven clustering. Validation: (i) analytic and DES are directionally consistent and agree in magnitude where both are defined — the analytic stable-zone p99 (69 s) prices only the stable zones while DES p99 (1791 s) carries the unstable P/R/X pools, which is exactly the heavy-tail signature the analytic 'stable=False' flags; (ii) calibration is transparent (per-column fits with n, cv, and KS p-values in logs/analysis_baseline.log; the belt fit is strongest, n=29, cv=0.49); (iii) SLA anchoring: M1+M2 DES p99=1626 s passes the 1800 s standard-lane line (baseline 1791 s sits at the line) but the 600 s Pre-Check line requires P5 plus P1/P3 together. Strengths: clean bottleneck localization (ρ ranking with a structural explanation for the Pre-Check paradox), every modification traceable to a bottleneck, hybrid cross-validation, interpretable sensitivity. Weaknesses: 9.9-minute sample → high uncertainty on X-ray (n=11) and D-zone parameters; M/M/c underestimates heavy tails for non-exponential services (partially mitigated by Kingman + DES); the absolute operating point is an anchored assumption, not an observation; no balking/rerouting or cross-zone walk times modeled; the flexible controller is a static rule, and at the base point the demand exceeds total capacity so M1 alone cannot make the network stable (an honest structural limit: M1+M2 is the best combined result, 705 s mean / 1626 s p99). Future work: longer multi-airport data windows to firm up X-ray/D parameters; online ρ estimation with MDP-based lane control; a queueing network with balking and rerouting; the smart-belt ±20% bag-batch time case as a third modification; field surveys to calibrate the stylized cultural factors; Pre-Check enrollment dynamics (the $85/5-yr price and ~45% enrollment suggest the P-class share will drift, making P5 a recurring rebalancing problem).
